payload.title: Taylor's Promise of Shared Prosperity and the Reorganization of Factory Work, c. 1900-1939
payload.set_intro:
Historical source (real document)
(primary source)
The Principles of Scientific Management, ch. I (opening)
Frederick Winslow Taylor, American mechanical engineer, 1911 (New York: Harper & Brothers). Project Gutenberg eBook #6435. Reuse: public domain in the United States (published before 1929). excerpted (1 segment); whitespace normalized; no wording changed.
Context: Frederick W. Taylor was an American engineer who published this book in 1911 about how to organize work in factories.

"The principal object of management should be to secure the maximum prosperity for the employer, coupled with the maximum prosperity for each employee. The words "maximum prosperity" are used, in their broad sense, to mean not only large dividends for the company or owner, but the development of every branch of the business to its highest state of excellence, so that the prosperity may be permanent. In the same way maximum prosperity for each employee means not only higher wages than are usually received by men of his class, but, of more importance still, it also means the development of each man to his state of maximum efficiency, so that he may be able to do, generally speaking, the highest grade of work for which his natural abilities fit him, and it further means giving him, when possible, this class of work to do. It would seem to be so self-evident that maximum prosperity for the employer, coupled with maximum prosperity for the employee, ought to be the two leading objects of management, that even to state this fact should be unnecessary. And yet there is no question that, throughout the industrial world, a large part of the organization of employers, as well as employees, is for war rather than for peace, and that perhaps the majority on either side do not believe that it is possible so to arrange their mutual relations that their interests become identical."

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE claim Taylor makes in the excerpt about the relationship between employers and employees.
parts.model_answer: Taylor claims that the main goal of management should be the maximum prosperity of the employer together with the maximum prosperity of each employee.

rubric_rows.criterion: Describe one claim from the excerpt about employer-employee relations, such as that management should seek maximum prosperity for both sides, that employee prosperity means higher wages and work suited to each man's abilities, that the two sides' interests can become identical, or that employers and workers are currently organized for war rather than peace.
required_elements: Taylor claims that the main goal of management should be the maximum prosperity of the employer together with the maximum prosperity of each employee.

Taylor claims that prosperity for the worker means more than higher wages: it also means developing each man to his maximum efficiency and giving him the highest grade of work his natural abilities fit him for.
Taylor argues that the interests of employers and employees can become identical, even though most people on both sides do not believe this.
Taylor observes that across the industrial world employers and employees are organized 'for war rather than for peace,' so their relations are currently marked by conflict.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific historical development in the period 1900-1939 that either supports or challenges Taylor's claim that the interests of employers and employees could become identical.
parts.model_answer: Supports: In 1914 Henry Ford introduced the Five Dollar Day, roughly doubling pay for many workers at his Highland Park plant after the moving assembly line (1913) raised output, which suggested that higher productivity could bring higher wages and higher profits together.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explain one specific development from 1900-1939 that supports Taylor's claim (for example, higher wages tied to new production methods) or challenges it (for example, strikes, union organizing, or worker resistance to time study and speedups), and connect it to the idea of shared or conflicting interests.
required_elements: Supports: In 1914 Henry Ford introduced the Five Dollar Day, roughly doubling pay for many workers at his Highland Park plant after the moving assembly line (1913) raised output, which suggested that higher productivity could bring higher wages and higher profits together.

Challenges: Workers at the Watertown Arsenal in Massachusetts went on strike in 1911 to protest stopwatch time study, and the dispute led to congressional hearings on the Taylor system, showing that many workers saw scientific management as a speedup that served employers.

Challenges: Assembly-line work at Ford was so repetitive and tightly paced that the company had very high worker turnover around 1913, which shows that the new methods did not automatically win workers' loyalty.

Challenges: The 1936-1937 sit-down strike at General Motors plants in Flint, Michigan, led by the United Auto Workers, showed continuing conflict between mass-production workers and employers over pay, pace of work, and union recognition.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE way that scientific management or assembly-line methods were adopted or adapted in Europe or the Soviet Union in the period 1900-1939.
parts.model_answer: In 1918 Lenin publicly called for the Soviet state to study and adopt the Taylor system, even though he also criticized it as a capitalist method, because he wanted to raise labor productivity.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explain one specific example of scientific management or assembly-line methods being adopted or adapted in Europe or the Soviet Union between 1900 and 1939, such as Lenin's 1918 endorsement of the Taylor system, Soviet industrialization under the Five-Year Plans and the Stakhanovite movement, Ford's help building the Soviet automobile plant at Nizhny Novgorod (Gorky), the Weimar German rationalization movement, or assembly-line production at Citroen or Fiat.
required_elements: In 1918 Lenin publicly called for the Soviet state to study and adopt the Taylor system, even though he also criticized it as a capitalist method, because he wanted to raise labor productivity.

Under the Five-Year Plans beginning in 1928, the Soviet Union pushed rapid industrialization and production quotas, and from 1935 the Stakhanovite movement celebrated workers who greatly exceeded output targets.

Under an agreement signed in 1929, the Ford Motor Company helped the Soviet Union build a large automobile plant at Nizhny Novgorod (later Gorky), which brought American assembly-line methods to Soviet industry.
In Weimar Germany in the 1920s, industrialists and engineers promoted 'rationalization,' using standardization, time study, and mechanized production to rebuild industry after the First World War.
French carmaker Citroen began mass production on the American model in 1919, and Fiat in Italy opened its Lingotto factory in Turin in the 1920s, designed around assembly-line production.

Sample response, high score (3/3; Part A 1, Part B 1, Part C 1):
(A) Taylor claims that the main goal of management should be "maximum prosperity" for both the employer and each employee at once. He argues that for workers this means not just higher wages but being trained to their highest efficiency and given the best grade of work they are fit for, so the two sides' interests could become identical instead of being organized "for war."

(B) The Ford Motor Company's five-dollar day, introduced in 1914, partly supports Taylor's claim. After Ford adopted the moving assembly line at Highland Park in 1913, turnover was very high because the work was monotonous, so Ford roughly doubled the usual daily wage. This lowered turnover and raised productivity for the company, and workers earned much more, so both sides seemed to gain from efficient production the way Taylor predicted. However, Ford's workers still had little control over the pace of the line, which shows the interests were not completely identical.

(C) In Soviet Russia, Lenin publicly endorsed the Taylor system in 1918, arguing that the Soviet state should adopt its scientific methods of organizing labor while rejecting its capitalist exploitation. Later, during Stalin's Five-Year Plans, the state adapted these ideas to push for higher output through the Stakhanovite movement, which began in 1935 when the miner Alexei Stakhanov was celebrated for far exceeding his coal quota. This shows that the Soviets used efficiency methods to serve state industrialization goals rather than private profit.
   - "the main goal of management should be "maximum prosperity" for both the employer and each employee at once" - Earns the point: correctly describes a claim from the excerpt about employer-employee relations.
   - "so the two sides' interests could become identical instead of being organized "for war."" - Adds accurate detail tying the claim to the excerpt's 'war rather than peace' line.
   - "The Ford Motor Company's five-dollar day, introduced in 1914" - Specific, accurate development within 1900-1939; Ford examples are allowed.
   - "both sides seemed to gain from efficient production the way Taylor predicted" - Earns the point: links the development directly to Taylor's claim of shared interests.
   - "Lenin publicly endorsed the Taylor system in 1918" - Specific, accurate Soviet adoption of scientific management within the period.
   - "Stakhanovite movement, which began in 1935" - Earns the point: explains how the method was adapted for state industrialization, with an accurate date and example.

Sample response, middle score (2/3; Part A 1, Part B 0, Part C 1):
(A) Taylor claims that the best goal for management is to get the maximum prosperity for the employer and the maximum prosperity for each employee at the same time. He says that for workers this means higher wages than usual and also being trained to do the best kind of work that fits their abilities, so the employer and the worker do not have to be enemies.

(B) During this time period there were a lot of problems between workers and bosses in factories, and this challenges what Taylor said. Many workers did not like the new methods and thought the bosses only cared about making more money. This shows that the interests of employers and employees were not really identical like Taylor thought, because both sides were still fighting with each other.

(C) One way scientific management was adopted outside the United States was in the Soviet Union. Lenin supported the Taylor system in 1918 because the new Soviet government wanted to build up industry quickly after the revolution. Later, under Stalin's Five-Year Plans starting in 1928, the Soviets used American-style mass production methods in their factories, and the Soviet Union even worked with the Ford Motor Company to build an auto plant at Nizhny Novgorod. This shows the Soviets adapted capitalist production methods to fit their communist goals of fast industrialization.
   - "the maximum prosperity for the employer and the maximum prosperity for each employee at the same time" - Accurately describes a claim actually made in the excerpt about employers and employees, so Part A earns the point.
   - "higher wages than usual and also being trained to do the best kind of work that fits their abilities" - Adds correct detail from the excerpt about what employee prosperity means, which strengthens the Part A claim.
   - "During this time period there were a lot of problems between workers and bosses in factories" - Too vague: it names no specific event, strike, union, or practice from 1900-1939, so Part B does not earn the point.
   - "Many workers did not like the new methods and thought the bosses only cared about making more money." - Gestures at worker resistance and links to conflicting interests, but there is no specific, datable development such as a particular strike or union action. Missing evidence costs the point.
   - "Lenin supported the Taylor system in 1918" - Specific, accurate example of adoption in the Soviet Union within 1900-1939.

Sample response, low score (1/3; Part A 1, Part B 0, Part C 0):
(A) Taylor claims that the main goal of management should be to get the maximum prosperity for the employer and also the maximum prosperity for each employee at the same time. He says that for workers this means higher wages than other men of his class usually get, and also that each man is developed to his highest efficiency and given the kind of work that fits his natural abilities. He also says that a lot of employers and employees see each other as being at war instead of working together.

(B) During the early 1900s there were a lot of problems in factories in America. Workers worked long hours and the factories were crowded and sometimes dangerous. Many workers were unhappy about how they were treated and this caused problems for the whole country. This shows that employers and employees did not always get along, so it was hard for their interests to be the same.

(C) Scientific management was used in other places too. Many countries in Europe saw how well America was doing with its factories and wanted to copy these methods to make more goods. They used the new ideas about efficiency in their own factories so that they could compete with the United States. This helped industry grow in Europe in the early 1900s.
   - "get the maximum prosperity for the employer and also the maximum prosperity for each employee at the same time" - Accurately describes a claim actually made in the excerpt about employer-employee relations, so Part A earns its point.
   - "a lot of employers and employees see each other as being at war instead of working together" - Correct paraphrase of Taylor's 'war rather than peace' line; reinforces the Part A point.
   - "Workers worked long hours and the factories were crowded and sometimes dangerous." - Too general: names no specific strike, union, law, firm, or event from 1900-1939, so it is not a specific historical development.
   - "This shows that employers and employees did not always get along, so it was hard for their interests to be the same." - Links to the idea of conflicting interests, but the link is attached to vague background, not an identifiable development, so no point.
   - "Many countries in Europe saw how well America was doing with its factories and wanted to copy these methods" - Only a general 'other countries copied America' statement; no specific country, firm, or program (such as the Soviet Union, Weimar Germany, Fiat, or Citroen), which the rubric note says does not earn the point.
   - "This helped industry grow in Europe in the early 1900s." - Vague outcome with no evidence or explanation of how the methods were adopted or adapted.

facts: Frederick Winslow Taylor published The Principles of Scientific Management in 1911.
Scientific management used time and motion study, standardized tasks, and incentive pay to raise output per worker.
Ford introduced a moving assembly line at its Highland Park, Michigan, plant in 1913.

Mass production lowered the price of the Model T over the 1910s, making cars available to many more consumers.
Lenin endorsed studying and applying the Taylor system in 1918.
The first Soviet Five-Year Plan began in 1928; the Stakhanovite movement began in 1935.
The Flint sit-down strike against General Motors took place in 1936-1937.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE way the print portrays the relationship between people and the natural world.
parts.model_answer: The print shows the boatmen as small and helpless beneath a wave that rises far above them and looks ready to crash down on their narrow boats.

rubric_rows.criterion: Describe ONE way the image shows people in relation to nature, based on what is visible: the huge wave dwarfing three narrow boats, the rowers crouched low, the distant Mount Fuji appearing small and calm beneath the wave, or the low horizon that makes the human figures seem fragile.
required_elements: The print shows the boatmen as small and helpless beneath a wave that rises far above them and looks ready to crash down on their narrow boats.
The rowers crouch low in their boats while the foam of the wave curls like claws above them, suggesting the danger and power of the sea.
Mount Fuji appears small and calm in the distance, framed by the wave, so the natural world dominates the scene and the people seem fragile within it.
The low horizon and huge swells put the human figures at the mercy of nature, showing people working in a dangerous environment rather than controlling it.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE economic or social development in Japan in the period 1750 to 1853 that helps explain why woodblock prints such as this one could be produced and sold widely.
parts.model_answer: The growth of large cities such as Edo created a large population of merchants and artisans with money to spend on affordable entertainment and decoration, including woodblock prints.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explain ONE development in Japan from 1750 to 1853 that made mass production or broad sale of prints possible, such as the growth of large commercial cities like Edo, a wealthier merchant and townsperson population, the inexpensive multi-block printing process run by commercial publishers, or the limited foreign trade at Nagasaki that brought in goods such as imported pigment.
required_elements: The growth of large cities such as Edo created a large population of merchants and artisans with money to spend on affordable entertainment and decoration, including woodblock prints.
Commercial publishers used the multi-block color printing process to produce many copies of a design cheaply, so prints could be sold in large numbers to townspeople.

Limited Dutch and Chinese trade at Nagasaki brought in foreign goods such as the imported blue pigment used in prints of this period, along with some knowledge of Western techniques like linear perspective.
Peace and internal stability under the Tokugawa shogunate supported domestic travel and commerce, which helped create demand for prints of famous places such as Mount Fuji.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE way that cultural exchange between Japan and Europe changed in the period 1853 to 1900.
parts.model_answer: After the Perry expedition and the treaties of the 1850s opened Japanese ports, Japanese prints and other goods were exported to Europe, where collectors created a fashion known as Japonisme.

rubric_rows.criterion: Explain ONE change in cultural exchange between Japan and Europe from 1853 to 1900, such as the opening of Japan after the Perry expedition and the treaties that followed, the export of Japanese prints and the European fashion called Japonisme, Japanese displays at world's fairs such as the 1867 Paris exhibition, or Meiji adoption of Western art, education, and technology.
required_elements: After the Perry expedition and the treaties of the 1850s opened Japanese ports, Japanese prints and other goods were exported to Europe, where collectors created a fashion known as Japonisme.
European artists such as Vincent van Gogh copied or studied Japanese woodblock prints in the 1880s, borrowing flat color and bold outlines.
Japan displayed its art and crafts at world's fairs such as the 1867 Paris Exposition Universelle, giving European audiences direct contact with Japanese goods.
After the Meiji Restoration of 1868, the Japanese government adopted Western technology, schooling, and art training, so European styles and ideas flowed into Japan.

Scoring guide (ALTON reference — not official AP scoring). This question is worth 3 points.
Part A (0-1): Describe ONE way the image shows people in relation to nature, based on what is visible: the huge wave dwarfing three narrow boats, the rowers crouched low, the distant Mount Fuji appearing small and calm beneath the wave, or the low horizon that makes the human figures seem fragile.
   - 1: The response accurately describes ONE way the print relates people to nature, such as showing the boatmen as small and vulnerable beneath a much larger, threatening wave.
   - 0: The response does not describe a feature of the image that relates people to nature, or only restates the title or names the artist.
Part B (0-1): Explain ONE development in Japan from 1750 to 1853 that made mass production or broad sale of prints possible, such as the growth of large commercial cities like Edo, a wealthier merchant and townsperson population, the inexpensive multi-block printing process run by commercial publishers, or the limited foreign trade at Nagasaki that brought in goods such as imported pigment.
   - 1: The response explains ONE specific development in Japan from 1750 to 1853 and connects it to the production or sale of prints such as this one.
   - 0: The response names no relevant development, uses a development from outside 1750 to 1853, or only describes the image again.
Part C (0-1): Explain ONE change in cultural exchange between Japan and Europe from 1853 to 1900, such as the opening of Japan after the Perry expedition and the treaties that followed, the export of Japanese prints and the European fashion called Japonisme, Japanese displays at world's fairs such as the 1867 Paris exhibition, or Meiji adoption of Western art, education, and technology.
   - 1: The response explains ONE specific change in cultural exchange between Japan and Europe from 1853 to 1900.
   - 0: The response gives no relevant change, stays outside 1853 to 1900, or makes only a general statement that Japan and Europe had contact.
Note: Each part earns 1 point, for a total of 3 points; parts are scored independently.
Note: For Part A, accept any accurate reading of the visible image; do not require students to identify the boats' purpose or translate the inscription.
Note: For Part B, mention of Dutch and Chinese trade at Nagasaki earns the point only if it is connected to prints, materials, or ideas, such as imported blue pigment or knowledge of Western perspective.
Note: For Part C, the exchange may run in either direction: Japanese art influencing Europe or European ideas and goods entering Meiji Japan.
Note: Do not award credit for claims that Japanese prints alone caused Impressionism or any other European art movement; influence on particular artists is acceptable.

Sample response, high score (3/3; Part A 1, Part B 1, Part C 1):
(A) The print shows people as small and helpless next to nature. The huge wave with claw-like foam curls over three narrow boats, and the rowers are crouched low in them as if they are just holding on. Even Mount Fuji looks tiny in the background, so the overall message is that nature is far more powerful than the humans in it.

(B) During the Tokugawa period, cities like Edo grew very large, and a wealthy class of merchants and townspeople (chonin) developed because of commercial growth during the long peace. These townspeople had money and leisure to spend on entertainment and art, so commercial publishers could print many cheap copies of prints like Hokusai's using carved woodblocks and sell them to a big urban market. This demand from the merchant class is a big reason why ukiyo-e prints were mass produced and sold widely.

(C) After Commodore Perry arrived in 1853 and Japan signed treaties opening its ports, cultural exchange became much more open in both directions. Japanese prints were exported to Europe and became popular with collectors, starting a fashion called Japonisme, and artists like Vincent van Gogh collected and copied ukiyo-e prints. At the same time, the Meiji government sent officials abroad and brought in Western education, technology, and art styles, so exchange moved from the limited Dutch trade at Nagasaki to wide, two-way contact.
   - "The huge wave with claw-like foam curls over three narrow boats, and the rowers are crouched low" - Describes visible features accurately and ties them to the people-nature relationship (humans vulnerable to nature). Earns the point.
   - "a wealthy class of merchants and townspeople (chonin) developed" - Names a specific development from 1750-1853 (urban growth and a richer merchant class).
   - "commercial publishers could print many cheap copies of prints like Hokusai's using carved woodblocks and sell them to a big urban market" - Links the development directly to producing and selling prints, which the rubric requires. Earns the point.
   - "Japanese prints were exported to Europe and became popular with collectors, starting a fashion called Japonisme" - Gives a specific change in cultural exchange in 1853-1900 and correctly places it after the treaties opened Japan.
   - "artists like Vincent van Gogh collected and copied ukiyo-e prints" - Accurate example of influence on one particular artist, with no claim that prints alone caused a whole art movement. Supports the point.

Sample response, middle score (2/3; Part A 1, Part B 1, Part C 0):
(A) The print shows people as small and weak compared to nature. The huge wave curls high over the three boats and looks like it has claws, while the rowers are crouched low in the boats and look tiny. Mount Fuji is far away in the background and looks small too, so the wave is the biggest thing in the picture and the people seem like they could be swallowed up by it.

(B) Under the Tokugawa, Japan had a lot of peace and cities like Edo grew very large. Merchants and townspeople there made money and had spare cash, so they bought things for fun and culture, and publishers could sell prints to them cheaply because many copies could be printed from the woodblocks. This is why a print like The Great Wave was able to sell so widely.

(C) After 1853 Japan and Europe had more contact and things changed a lot. Japan and Europe traded and exchanged ideas and Japan became more connected to the world. Both sides learned about each other more than before and this had an effect on culture and art.
   - "The huge wave curls high over the three boats and looks like it has claws, while the rowers are crouched low in the boats and look tiny." - Accurate description of visible features (huge wave, tiny crouched rowers) showing people as vulnerable to nature. Earns the point.
   - "The print shows people as small and weak compared to nature." - Clear claim about the people-nature relationship, supported by the details that follow.
   - "Under the Tokugawa, Japan had a lot of peace and cities like Edo grew very large." - Names a relevant development within 1750 to 1853: the growth of Edo as a large commercial city under the Tokugawa.
   - "Merchants and townspeople there made money and had spare cash, so they bought things for fun and culture, and publishers could sell prints to them cheaply because many copies could be printed from the woodblocks." - Connects a wealthier urban population and commercial publishing to broad sale of prints. Explanation is brief but linked to production and sale, so it earns the point.
   - "After 1853 Japan and Europe had more contact and things changed a lot." - Only a general statement that contact increased. It does not name the Perry expedition, treaties, Japonisme, world's fairs, or Meiji Westernization, so no specific change is explained.
   - "Both sides learned about each other more than before and this had an effect on culture and art." - Vague and lacks specific evidence or a described change in exchange. It needs a concrete example, such as Japanese prints influencing particular European artists or Meiji adoption of Western technology. No credit.

Sample response, low score (1/3; Part A 1, Part B 0, Part C 0):
(A) The print shows people as very small and weak compared to nature. The big wave curls up over the three boats and the men rowing are crouched down low, so the wave looks much bigger and more powerful than they are. Mount Fuji in the back looks tiny and calm next to it.

(B) During this time Japan was doing a lot of things that helped art. The shogunate was in charge and Japan had a lot of trade and culture. Hokusai was a famous artist so people wanted to buy his work and it spread around Japan. This is why prints like The Great Wave could be sold in many places.

(C) After 1853 Japan and Europe had more contact with each other. Europeans and Japanese people shared ideas and art and Japan became more connected to the world. This changed how the two places saw each other and there was a lot of exchange between them in the later 1800s.
   - "The big wave curls up over the three boats and the men rowing are crouched down low, so the wave looks much bigger and more powerful than they are." - Accurately describes visible features (huge wave, small crouched rowers) and ties them to people being vulnerable before nature. Earns the point.
   - "The shogunate was in charge and Japan had a lot of trade and culture." - Too vague. It names no specific development such as Edo's growth, a wealthy merchant class, or commercial publishers, and does not explain how it made prints cheap or widely sold. No credit.
   - "Hokusai was a famous artist so people wanted to buy his work and it spread around Japan." - This only restates the source context and the artist's fame. It is not an economic or social development from 1750 to 1853.
   - "After 1853 Japan and Europe had more contact with each other." - Only a general statement that the two had contact. It does not mention the Perry expedition, Japonisme, world's fairs, or Meiji adoption of Western ideas, so no specific change is explained.
   - "Europeans and Japanese people shared ideas and art and Japan became more connected to the world." - Vague and unsupported. It gives no specific example, event, or direction of exchange, so it cannot earn the point.

common_pitfalls: In Part A, naming the artist, date, or title without describing how people and nature appear in the image.
In Part A, asserting details about the boats' cargo or purpose that the image does not show.
In Part B, using the Perry expedition or Meiji reforms, which fall outside 1750 to 1853.
In Part B, describing the wave or Mount Fuji again instead of a historical development.
In Part C, writing only that Japan and Europe traded, without a specific change or example.
In Part C, claiming Japanese prints single-handedly created Impressionism.
Describing Tokugawa Japan as completely closed, ignoring regulated trade at Nagasaki.
facts: Katsushika Hokusai designed Under the Wave off Kanagawa around 1831 as part of a series of views of Mount Fuji.
Color woodblock prints in Edo-period Japan were made by carving separate blocks for different colors, which allowed many copies to be printed at a relatively low price.
Edo (Tokyo) was among the largest cities in the world in the 1700s, with a large population of merchants and artisans.
Under Tokugawa policy, regulated foreign trade was carried on chiefly through Nagasaki, where Dutch merchants were confined to Dejima and Chinese merchants also traded.
Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment first made in Europe, was imported into Japan and used in prints of this period, including this one.
Commodore Matthew Perry's expedition (1853 to 1854) led to the Treaty of Kanagawa, and later treaties opened more Japanese ports to Western trade.
The Meiji Restoration of 1868 began a government program of Westernization and industrialization.
Japan exhibited at the 1867 Paris Exposition Universelle.
European artists such as Vincent van Gogh and Claude Monet collected or copied Japanese woodblock prints in the later 1800s; this European taste was called Japonisme.

annotations.comment: Too vague. It names no specific development such as Edo's growth, a wealthy merchant class, or commercial publishers, and does not explain how it made prints cheap or widely sold. No credit.

annotations.quote: Hokusai was a famous artist so people wanted to buy his work and it spread around Japan.
annotations.comment: This only restates the source context and the artist's fame. It is not an economic or social development from 1750 to 1853.

annotations.quote: After 1853 Japan and Europe had more contact with each other.
annotations.comment: Only a general statement that the two had contact. It does not mention the Perry expedition, Japonisme, world's fairs, or Meiji adoption of Western ideas, so no specific change is explained.

annotations.quote: Europeans and Japanese people shared ideas and art and Japan became more connected to the world.
annotations.comment: Vague and unsupported. It gives no specific example, event, or direction of exchange, so it cannot earn the point.
